clue.text: Festival — it's charms re-evaluated?

indicators.note: something re-evaluated is reworked and set out afresh, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the contraction is spelt out as its three letters

explanation.surface: Someone at a festival wonders whether its charms deserve a second look.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-evaluated' rearranges the letters of IT'S plus CHARMS.
explanation.definitionFit: The December holiday is one of the great Christian feast days.

clue.text: Highbrow British tucking into breakfast food

indicators.note: one piece tucks itself inside the other, so it is placed within the breakfast word

parts.note: cereal is a typical breakfast food

explanation.surface: A Briton is tucking into the morning cereal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures someone eating breakfast, but 'tucking into' is a container signal, not eating.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe an intellectual, thinking-heavy taste or person.

clue.text: River (hard one to solve!)

parts.note: H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard
taken as written

explanation.surface: A setter jokes that this river makes a tough clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue works twice: R, H and ONE build the French river, while the bracket jokes about how hard it is to crack.
explanation.definitionFit: The great river flows from the Swiss Alps through Lyon to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: How to prepare a lot of brandies without thinking

definitions.text: How to prepare a lot of brandies
definitions.meaning: read as two words, the answer is an instruction: jumble most of the word brandies, its final S dropped, to get its second half

explanation.surface: A bartender mixes a round of brandies on autopilot.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is cryptic: 'a lot of brandies' is BRANDIE, and its letters scattered make BRAINED, the second half of the answer. The second definition is plain.
explanation.definitionFit: A muddled, forgetful person acts heedlessly, and the first half playfully instructs mixing up most of a word.

clue.text: Scots leader to risk interrupting physicist

indicators.note: one word breaks into the middle of the other, so it is placed inside the scientist's name

parts.note: Ernst Mach was an Austrian physicist, remembered in the Mach number
to bet is to risk money on an outcome

explanation.surface: A Scottish chief stakes money while a scientist is talking.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Scots leader' is Shakespeare's Scottish king; Ernst Mach was an Austrian physicist, remembered in the Mach number.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's tragic protagonist seizes the throne and rules Scotland as king.

clue.text: Inattentive captain?

parts.note: a ship's commander, read playfully as someone who skips over things and doesn't pay attention

explanation.surface: A ship's master who never pays attention.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a ship's captain, and literally one who skips, missing bits out.

clue.text: Peak, one seen around top of Matterhorn

indicators.note: the first piece goes around the second, so it surrounds the mountain's first letter

parts.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards

indicators.note: the top of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A climber reaches the summit of the Matterhorn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' wraps ACE around M, the first letter of Matterhorn.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean the highest point or culmination of something.

clue.text: Alcohol producing malingering, we hear

indicators.note: signals that the word wanted sounds like the phrase given, said out loud

parts.note: a malingerer fakes illness, putting on a sham pain

explanation.surface: A drinker blames the bubbly for fake sickness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear' says SHAM PAIN, a fake ache, is spoken like the sparkling wine.
explanation.definitionFit: The sparkling wine from north-east France is an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Diarist still penning start of last year

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, so one piece holds the others inside it

parts.note: even and still both intensify a comparison (even better, still better)

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: A diarist is still writing up the beginning of last year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' puts L (the start of 'last') and Y inside EVEN. John Evelyn kept a famous 17th-century diary.
explanation.definitionFit: John Evelyn, contemporary of Pepys, is known chiefly for his diary.

clue.text: I produce depression with one lie about a result of police parade

parts.note: a dent is a small hollow or depression
I is the Roman numeral one

indicators.note: the lie goes about, that is around, the single letter

parts.note: fiction is an untruth

explanation.surface: Someone sinks into gloom over a lie they told about a line-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts A inside FICTION. A police parade here is an identity parade, or line-up, of suspects.
explanation.definitionFit: A line-up exists so that a witness can pick out the culprit, naming who did it.

clue.text: Girl's mostly to love enthralling hearts on the rebound

indicators.note: something rebounding comes back, so the built word is read backwards
to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds the other inside
mostly means losing the final letter

parts.note: to adore is to love deeply
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games

explanation.surface: A girl, jilted, still mostly loves the heart-throb she rebounds from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' cuts ADORE to ADOR; 'enthralling' puts H inside it, giving ADOHR, and 'on the rebound' turns that round.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a female given name, as in the sitcom character Rhoda Morgenstern.

clue.text: Not entirely smart version of cradle could be used in this

indicators.note: not entirely means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: chic means stylish or smart

indicators.note: a version of a word is a reworking of it, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A stylish redesign of a baby's cot is meant for a nursery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'version of' rearranges the cradle's letters. The definition leans on the rest of the clue: a cradle could be used in looking after children, a semi-&lit.
explanation.definitionFit: Looking after little children is where a crib or cot comes into use.

clue.text: Swim round about — though you can't do it underwater!

indicators.note: one piece goes round the other, enclosing it

parts.note: to bathe is to swim
RE means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A swimmer is told to go round once more, but beware: no air below.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cryptic hint rather than a synonym: the one thing a swimmer cannot do below the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking in air through the lungs is impossible beneath the surface without equipment.

clue.text: Display work, including a new musical work

indicators.note: the first piece includes, so contains, the others

parts.note: to ply a trade is to work at it
OP, short for opus, numbers a composer's works

explanation.surface: An exhibition piece includes a newly composed score.
explanation.walkthrough: OP, short for opus, is the standard crossword shorthand for a musical work.
explanation.definitionFit: A panoply is an impressive array, a splendid show of many things.

clue.text: Old royal gent with queen's jewellery is a hero in opera

parts.note: Prince Albert was Queen Victoria's consort
her, the possessive, stands for the queen's
a ring is a piece of jewellery

explanation.surface: Victoria's husband, wearing her jewels, is the star of an opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Albert Herring is the title hero of Benjamin Britten's comic opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Britten's 1947 comic opera is named after its unlikely protagonist, a shy greengrocer's boy.

clue.text: Revert to earlier stance as diocese initially invested in second set of bells

parts.note: to second is to back a proposal

indicators.note: to be invested in is to be placed inside, so the letter goes within the bells

parts.note: a peal is a set of bells rung together

indicators.note: initially means the first letter is taken

explanation.surface: A diocese reverses its position after putting money into a new peal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'invested in' puts D, the first letter of 'diocese', inside PEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To pedal backwards is to retreat from or withdraw a position previously held.

clue.text: Devotee to attempt following fashionable soldiers

indicators.note: following sends the devotee and attempt pieces after the fashionable piece, though the clue names them first

parts.note: in means in fashion
a fan is a devotee
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: A fan of fashion is keen to try to keep up with the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fan trying to keep up with fashion; in fact 'soldiers' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Foot soldiers make up this branch of an army.

clue.text: Badly repairing core form of airmail

indicators.note: something done badly is mangled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is botching the repair of the central part of a postal system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges REPAIRING CORE.
explanation.definitionFit: Trained birds have carried messages through the air for centuries.

clue.text: Sex-appeal gets chap embracing one from a Mediterranean country

parts.note: it is an old slang word for sex appeal

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold, so the name holds the letter inside it

parts.note: Alan is a typical man's name
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A charming man hugs someone from Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embracing' puts I inside ALAN. 'It' for sex appeal comes from the 1920s 'It girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things native to Italy, a southern European peninsula.

clue.text: Scientist to decline after taking in new information

indicators.note: taking in means enclosing, so the decay word swallows the letter

parts.note: to rot is to decay or decline
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A scientist declines after taking in new facts.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British informal slang for information. Wilhelm Röntgen discovered X-rays.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilhelm Röntgen was the German physicist who discovered X-rays.

clue.text: An evil event associated with a theatre of war

parts.note: a crime is a wicked act

explanation.surface: A wicked deed is linked to a battleground.
explanation.walkthrough: The Crimea was the setting of the Crimean War of the 1850s.
explanation.definitionFit: The peninsula on the Black Sea has repeatedly been fought over, notably in the 1850s war.

clue.text: Lace with rip, ruined? Enough to make you spit!

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: Torn lace makes a dressmaker furious enough to spit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges LACE and RIP. The definition plays on 'the spitting image', an exact likeness.
explanation.definitionFit: An exact copy is 'the spitting image' of its original.

clue.text: A river repeatedly ebbs and falls

indicators.note: an ebbing tide flows back, so the whole run of letters is read backwards

parts.note: again means once more, repeated

explanation.surface: A river keeps rising and falling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ebbs' turns round A, R and AGAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous cataracts on the US-Canada border are among the world's best-known waterfalls.

clue.text: French boyfriend snatching at violin

indicators.note: to snatch is to grab, so one word holds the other inside

parts.note: ami is French for friend or boyfriend

explanation.surface: A Frenchman grabs at an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Amati was a family of Cremona violin makers, so the name stands for one of their instruments.
explanation.definitionFit: Instruments made by the Amati family of Cremona are prized violins.

clue.text: Frustrating a drug-dealer's first association with hideout in China

indicators.note: the pieces sit in the porcelain word

parts.note: Ming is a famous Chinese dynasty and its porcelain

indicators.note: the first of a word is its initial letter

parts.note: a den is a hideout

explanation.surface: A drug dealer frustratingly uses a hideout in China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' means Ming porcelain or the Ming dynasty, not the country; 'first' takes the initial of 'drug-dealer's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both describe something that exasperates or infuriates.

clue.text: I doze before start of talk -not appropriate

parts.note: a nap is a short doze

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: I nod off before a talk begins, which is rude.
explanation.walkthrough: I, NAP and T (the start of 'talk') are put side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means unsuitable or out of place.

clue.text: Friendly power is jolly friendly if powerless

indicators.note: powerless means without P, the physics symbol for power

parts.note: pally means very friendly

explanation.surface: A friendly nation is jolly matey when weak.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the symbol for power, so PALLY without it.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation that sides with another in war or diplomacy is a supportive partner state.

clue.text: One new bird in New York, a person of no consequence

indicators.note: the pieces go in the abbreviation for the city

parts.note: a tit is a small bird

explanation.surface: A new bird turns up in Manhattan, unnoticed by anyone.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's 'New York' and 'new' both look like decoration, but each supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A nobody is someone insignificant who counts for little.
